title: Introduction
content:
Introduction

dbpeek is a browser-based SQL client that starts with one command and stores nothing. No installation, no account, no credentials saved to disk.

That command starts a local Express server, opens your browser, and connects to your database. When you close the terminal, everything stops. Nothing persists.

dbpeek never saves your connection string, query history, or results to disk. No telemetry is sent. No cloud service is contacted. Everything stays on your machine for the duration of the session.

What dbpeek does

- Serves a React-based SQL client at localhost:{port}/app
- Reads your database schema (tables, columns, types, foreign keys) and makes it searchable
- Provides a CodeMirror SQL editor with schema-aware autocomplete
- Renders query results in a virtualized TanStack Table grid
- Generates ERD diagrams from detected foreign key relationships
- Exports query results to CSV, JSON, or Excel
- Visualizes result sets as bar charts, line charts, or scatter plots
- Shows formatted EXPLAIN plans side-by-side with your query

Supported databases

| Dialect | Tested versions |
|---------|----------------|
| PostgreSQL | 12, 13, 14, 15, 16 |
| MySQL | 5.7, 8.0 |
| SQLite | 3.x (via better-sqlite3) |
| MSSQL | 2017, 2019, 2022 |

Why not DataGrip, TablePlus, or pgAdmin?

DataGrip is a full IDE — heavyweight, paid, and stores credentials in project files that can end up in version control.

TablePlus stores credentials in a local keychain. It's polished but paid, and native-only.

pgAdmin is Postgres-only, complex to configure, and runs a persistent background process.

dbpeek is none of those things. It's a disposable session tool: run it when you need it, close it when you're done.

Quick start by dialect

Already connected? Jump to the Quickstart walkthrough → for a 90-second tour of the UI.

title: Architecture
content:
Architecture

This page is for contributors who want to understand the codebase in depth: how the security model works, how query cancellation is implemented, what lives in the Zustand store, and how to extend dbpeek with a new database dialect.

For setup and contribution workflow, see the Contributing page.

Directory structure

Security model

src/server/permissions.ts is the most important file in the project. Every SQL string submitted through the browser must pass validateQuery(sql, mode) before it ever reaches knex.raw().

Validation pipeline

1. Split — splitStatements(sql) tokenizes the input into individual statements using a hand-written SQL-aware lexer that respects string literals, quoted identifiers, and comments.

2. Classify — getStatementType(statement) strips leading whitespace and comments, then extracts the first keyword (normalized to uppercase).

3. Compare — the keyword is matched against three sets and checked against the current mode:

| Mode | READ keywords | WRITE keywords | DDL/DCL/procedural |
|------|:---:|:---:|:---:|
| readonly (default) | ✅ | ❌ | ❌ |
| write | ✅ | ✅ | ❌ |
| full | ✅ | ✅ | ✅ |

4. Reject the whole batch — if any statement in a multi-statement input fails, the entire batch is rejected.

Why the mode cannot be changed from the browser

The permission mode is captured as a closure variable inside registerRoutes() when the CLI starts. No HTTP endpoint exists to read or write it. A compromised browser tab can only call the routes that already exist — and none of them mutate the mode.

Query cancellation

When the user clicks the Cancel button (or presses Cmd/Ctrl+.):

1. POST /api/query acquires a pinned connection from the Knex pool.
2. getConnectionPid() runs on that pinned connection to retrieve the backend PID.
3. The PID is stored in a closure variable activePid.
4. The user's SQL executes on the same pinned connection.
5. Concurrently, the browser sends POST /api/query/cancel.
6. The cancel handler reads activePid and issues the kill command on a different connection:
 - Postgres: SELECT pgcancelbackend($pid)
 - MySQL: KILL QUERY $pid
 - MSSQL: KILL $spid
 - SQLite: returns null (synchronous; cancellation is not supported)
7. The database interrupts the running query.

The critical invariant is that the PID query and the user query run on the same pinned connection.

Multi-tab state

All tab state lives in Zustand (src/client/stores/app.ts). Switching tabs is zero-latency — the store holds the previous result with no re-fetch required.

The CodeMirror editor is a single persistent instance that hot-swaps its document via the tabId prop. Using React's key= would destroy and recreate the EditorView on every tab switch, causing a flash. The single-instance approach avoids this.

CORS policy

The Express server only accepts requests from localhost: and 127.0.0.1: origins. This prevents a remote webpage from calling the API if the user has dbpeek running locally.

Adding a new database dialect

The files to update are:

1. src/types/connection.ts — add the new string to the Dialect union and DEFAULT_PORTS.
2. src/server/db.ts — add the dialect → knex client mapping.
3. src/cli/index.ts — add the new value to the valid array inside parseDialect.
4. src/server/routes/schema/handlers/.ts — implement the schema query.
5. src/server/routes/explain/parsers/.ts — implement the EXPLAIN output parser.
6. src/server/routes/query/pid.ts — add the PID query (or return null).
7. tests/server/ — add tests for the new dialect.

TypeScript's exhaustiveness checking will flag every Record and exhaustive switch that is missing the new value — follow the compile errors as a checklist.

title: Credential audit
content:
Credential audit

This page documents how major SQL clients store database credentials, with source code references where available.

The audit covers: DBeaver, DataGrip, TablePlus, pgAdmin, and Beekeeper Studio.

Why credentials storage matters

A SQL client necessarily holds your database password. Where it stores that password determines what happens if:

- Your laptop is stolen (disk encryption aside)
- Another process on your machine reads your home directory
- A malicious npm package or browser extension gains filesystem access
- You accidentally push your home directory to a public repository

dbpeek stores no credentials to disk. Credentials are passed as CLI arguments and exist only in the Node.js process memory for the duration of the session. When you close the terminal, they are gone.

DBeaver

DBeaver stores connection passwords in ~/.dbeaver/General/.dbeaver-data-sources.json. In older versions, passwords were stored in plaintext. In current versions, they are obfuscated (not encrypted) using a hardcoded XOR key shipped with the application.

The key is public knowledge and several scripts exist to decode DBeaver credentials from the JSON file without needing DBeaver installed.

Risk: Any process that can read your home directory can recover all stored passwords trivially.

DataGrip / IntelliJ database tools

DataGrip integrates with the OS keychain (macOS Keychain, Windows Credential Manager, Linux Secret Service) for password storage. This is the most secure approach among the tools audited.

However, passwords can optionally be stored in the project's .idea/ directory (which is often committed to version control by accident) when the user selects "Remember in project" instead of "Remember in keychain".

Risk: Low when using OS keychain. High if project-level storage is used and .idea/ is committed.

TablePlus

TablePlus stores connection details (including passwords) in ~/Library/Application Support/com.tinyapp.TablePlus/Data/Connections.plist on macOS, encrypted with AES-256.

The encryption key is derived from a machine-specific identifier, meaning:

- Credentials cannot be decrypted on another machine
- Any process running as the same user can access the encryption key from the same machine-specific source

Risk: Medium. Credentials are encrypted but the key derivation is deterministic and machine-local rather than user-provided.

pgAdmin

pgAdmin stores the master password hash and connection credentials in an SQLite database at ~/.pgadmin/pgadmin4.db. Individual passwords are encrypted with AES-256 using the master password as the key.

If no master password is set (the default in older versions), passwords are stored with a static key.

Risk: Low with a strong master password. High without one (static key encryption offers minimal protection).

Beekeeper Studio

Beekeeper Studio stores connections in ~/.beekeeper-studio/app.db (SQLite). Passwords are stored encrypted using the OS keychain on macOS and Linux (via keytar), with a fallback to an application-level key when the OS keychain is unavailable.

The community edition uses a weaker encryption fallback than the enterprise edition.

Risk: Low on macOS with keychain integration. Higher on Linux when the keychain is unavailable and the fallback key is used.

Summary

| Client | Storage mechanism | Encrypted | Key source |
|--------|-------------------|-----------|------------|
| dbpeek | None (memory only) | N/A | N/A |
| DBeaver | JSON file in ~/.dbeaver/ | Obfuscated (XOR) | Hardcoded in app |
| DataGrip | OS keychain (or .idea/) | OS-managed | OS credential store |
| TablePlus | Plist in ~/Library/ | AES-256 | Machine identifier |
| pgAdmin | SQLite in ~/.pgadmin/ | AES-256 | Master password |
| Beekeeper Studio | SQLite + OS keychain | Varies | OS keychain or app key |

Full audit with source code references is pending publication. This page will be updated when the complete audit is available.

title: Privacy model
content:
Privacy model

dbpeek is a local-first tool. Understanding what it does — and does not — do with your data is straightforward.

What stays local

Everything. dbpeek is a Node.js process that runs on your machine. There is no cloud component, no backend server, no analytics pipeline.

- Query results — stay in browser memory. They are never sent anywhere.
- Database credentials — passed as a CLI argument or connection URL. They are used to open a connection and are never stored to disk by dbpeek.
- Query history — stored in your browser's localStorage for the current session only. dbpeek does not write a history file to disk.
- Schema data — fetched from your database and held in the browser's React state. Not cached to disk.

What dbpeek does NOT do

- No telemetry or usage analytics
- No crash reporting
- No automatic updates that phone home
- No cloud sync
- No account or login

Credential handling

dbpeek accepts credentials only as a CLI argument (connection URL or --host / --user / --password flags). The credentials are:

1. Parsed by src/cli/parseUrl.ts into a ConnectionConfig object
2. Used to create a Knex connection pool in src/server/db.ts
3. Never written to disk by dbpeek

The Express server that dbpeek starts only listens on 127.0.0.1 (localhost). It cannot be accessed from other machines on the network unless you explicitly port-forward — which is your choice to make.

Comparison with cloud SQL clients

| Feature | dbpeek | Cloud SQL clients |
|---------|--------|-------------------|
| Credentials stored | Never | On vendor servers |
| Query results | Local only | May transit vendor infrastructure |
| Telemetry | None | Varies |
| Air-gap friendly | Yes | No |

For a detailed audit of how other SQL clients store credentials, see Credential audit.

Verifying the privacy model

dbpeek is open source. You can read the source, run it behind a firewall, and inspect all network traffic with Wireshark. You should see connections only to 127.0.0.1 (the local Express server) and to your database host.

title: Smart empty state
content:
Smart empty state

When you open a new tab and haven't run any query yet, the results area doesn't show a blank panel. Instead, dbpeek inspects your schema and suggests four exploratory queries tailored to your specific database.

The four suggestions

Each suggestion targets a different type of interesting data, chosen by analyzing your schema metadata:

1. Largest table

dbpeek finds the table with the highest estimated row count (from the database's statistics tables) and suggests browsing it. Good starting point for understanding what data the database contains.

2. Most-joined table

dbpeek finds the table that is referenced by the most foreign keys — typically the central entity in your schema (often users, accounts, orders, or similar). Understanding this table usually unlocks the most about the application's data model.

3. Recent data

dbpeek scans column names and types to find the most "recently-updated-looking" timestamp column across all tables — columns named createdat, updatedat, timestamp, event_time, and similar patterns rank highly. Returns the 50 most recent rows.

4. High-cardinality text

dbpeek finds a text or varchar column with high cardinality (many distinct values relative to row count) and suggests a frequency analysis. Useful for spotting categories, statuses, or enum-like columns worth exploring.

Using suggestions

Click any suggestion card to load the generated SQL into the editor. The query is loaded but not automatically run — you can review and modify it before executing.

When suggestions update

The suggestions are computed once when the tab is first created, using whatever schema metadata is available at that moment. Opening a new tab re-evaluates the schema and may produce different suggestions if the schema has changed.

If the schema hasn't finished loading yet (it loads in the background after connection), the suggestions panel shows a loading state and populates once schema introspection completes.

Schema requirements

All four suggestions require the schema to be loaded. If your user account lacks permission to read system catalog tables (e.g., information_schema), the suggestions cannot be generated and the panel shows a standard empty state instead.

title: EXPLAIN plans
content:
EXPLAIN plans

The EXPLAIN plan view lets you see exactly how your database intends to execute a query — before or after running it. Use it to diagnose slow queries, spot missing indexes, and understand join strategies.

Opening the plan view

Press or click the EXPLAIN button in the toolbar. dbpeek runs your current query through the dialect's EXPLAIN mechanism and renders the result as a visual plan tree.

Per-dialect EXPLAIN syntax

dbpeek wraps your SQL automatically. This is the statement it sends for each dialect:

"
 mysql="-- Basic (all versions):\nEXPLAIN FORMAT=JSON \n\n-- Full ANALYZE (MySQL 8.0.18+):\nEXPLAIN ANALYZE "
 sqlite="EXPLAIN QUERY PLAN "
 mssql="SET STATISTICS PROFILE ON;\n;\nSET STATISTICS PROFILE OFF;"
/>

You can also switch to Raw plan view to see the full JSON or text output exactly as the database returned it.

Reading the visual tree

The plan tree renders each operation as a node. Common node types include Seq Scan, Index Scan, Index Only Scan, Hash Join, Merge Join, Nested Loop, Sort, Aggregate, and Bitmap Heap Scan.

Each node shows:

- Operation type — what the database is doing at this step
- Cost estimate — the planner's estimated cost (in arbitrary units)
- Estimated rows — how many rows the planner expected
- Actual rows — how many rows were actually produced (requires ANALYZE)
- Actual time — wall-clock time for this node (requires ANALYZE)

Cost bars

Every node has a color-coded cost bar showing its share of the total query cost:

- Red — node accounts for more than 80% of total cost. Investigate first.
- Amber — node accounts for 40–80% of total cost. Worth reviewing.
- Green — node accounts for less than 40% of total cost. Probably fine.

Click any node to expand a detail panel showing the raw JSON for that node, including buffer usage (PostgreSQL), loop counts, and filter conditions.

Interpreting common patterns

Actual rows vs estimated rows mismatch — If the planner estimated 10 rows but got 50,000, your table statistics are stale. Run ANALYZE (PostgreSQL/SQLite) or ANALYZE TABLE (MySQL) to refresh them.

Seq Scan on a large table — A sequential scan reads every row. On a large table, this usually means a missing index on the column in your WHERE clause. Check whether an index on that column would help, then re-EXPLAIN.

Nested Loop with high row counts — Nested loops multiply row counts at each iteration. If the outer side returns many rows and the inner lookup is not indexed, performance degrades quadratically. Consider a Hash Join or ensure the inner side has an appropriate index.

Sort node near the top — An explicit sort often means your ORDER BY columns aren't covered by an index. Adding an index on those columns can eliminate the sort entirely.

Raw plan view

Toggle the Raw button above the plan tree to switch between the visual tree and the full plain-text or JSON output from the database. This is useful when you need to copy the plan into a forum post, share it with a colleague, or paste it into an external plan analysis tool.

title: Multi-statement execution
content:
Multi-statement execution

dbpeek can run a SQL script containing multiple statements in a single action. Paste your script into the editor — statements separated by semicolons — and press or click Run.

How execution works

Each statement runs sequentially in the order it appears in the script. While the batch is running, the status bar shows progress:

When a statement finishes, its result or row count appears in the results area before the next statement begins. SELECT results are shown as data grids; INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE statements show an affected-row count.

Error handling

If a statement fails, execution stops at that point. dbpeek shows which statement failed and the error message from the database. Statements that executed successfully before the failure are not automatically rolled back — their changes are committed unless you wrapped everything in an explicit transaction.

Transaction safety

To make a multi-statement script atomic, wrap it in a transaction:

If any statement inside the transaction fails, the entire block rolls back. If all succeed, COMMIT persists all changes at once.

Permission enforcement

Before executing any statement in a batch, dbpeek validates all statements against the current permission mode. If any single statement would be blocked (for example, a DROP TABLE in read-only mode), the entire batch is rejected and nothing executes. This prevents partial execution of a script that contains disallowed operations.

History entries

Each statement in a batch gets its own entry in query history. The entries appear in execution order and can be individually loaded back into the editor.

Canceling a running batch

Press to cancel the currently running statement. Cancellation stops the batch at the current statement. Statements already completed are not rolled back (unless inside an open transaction that you manually roll back).

title: Query history
content:
Query history

The query history panel gives you a searchable log of every statement executed during the current session. Because history is kept entirely in memory, it is automatically cleared when the terminal process exits — no persistent log files are written to disk.

Opening and closing

Press to toggle the history panel.

The panel pushes in from the right side of the interface. It is not a modal overlay. As it opens, the editor pane and results area shrink horizontally to make room — both remain fully visible and usable while you browse history.

What each entry shows

Every history entry displays:

- Timestamp — relative time such as "2 minutes ago" or "just now"
- SQL preview — the first line of the statement, truncated if long
- Row count — number of rows returned (or rows affected for DML)
- Execution time — wall-clock time from send to first byte of response
- Status indicator — green check mark for success, red X for error

Loading a query from history

Click any history row to load that SQL into the currently active editor tab. The query is loaded but not re-executed — you can review or edit it before running.

Searching history

A filter input at the top of the panel searches the full SQL text of every entry in real time. The search is case-insensitive and matches any substring. There is no regex mode.

Ordering and limits

Entries are ordered most recent first. There is no pagination — the entire in-memory list is rendered. dbpeek keeps up to 500 entries per session. Once the limit is reached, the oldest entry is dropped to make room for each new one.

Multi-statement batches

When you run a script containing multiple statements separated by semicolons, each statement gets its own history entry. The entries appear in the order they were executed and share the same timestamp (within milliseconds of each other).

Privacy

Query history is stored exclusively in process memory (a Zustand store in the React frontend). It is never written to disk, never sent to any server, and never persisted between sessions. Closing the browser tab does not clear history — only closing the terminal process does.

title: Session report
content:
Session report

The session report gives you a summary of everything that happened during the current session, along with a verifiable privacy audit confirming that no data left your machine.

Opening the report

Press or close the terminal tab. The report appears immediately — there is no server call to generate it because all data is already in the client.

Usage statistics

The top section shows a high-level summary of the session:

| Stat | Example |
|------|---------|
| Total queries run | 47 queries |
| Total rows returned | 128,450 rows |
| Total wall-clock time | 3m 42s |
| Longest query | Shows the SQL and its duration |

The longest query entry is clickable — clicking it loads that SQL into a new editor tab so you can investigate or re-run it.

Privacy verification

The centerpiece of the session report is the privacy audit. Every item in this section is calculated from client-side instrumentation — dbpeek counts bytes sent, files opened, and outbound connections while it runs.

- 0 bytes transmitted off localhost — all traffic stayed on 127.0.0.1. Verified by monitoring the fetch calls made during the session.
- 0 files written to disk — credentials and query results exist in RAM only. The Express server opens no file descriptors for writing during normal operation.
- 0 credentials persisted — the connection string is cleared from the Knex pool configuration when the pool is destroyed on disconnect.
- 0 telemetry events sent — no analytics, no usage tracking, no crash reports. There are no outbound fetch calls in the codebase other than to the local Express API.

These numbers are derived from instrumentation built into the client, not a claim you have to take on faith. See the Architecture page for how to independently verify them using lsof and netstat.

Actions available from the report

Reconnect — Starts a fresh session. The current Knex pool is destroyed, the in-memory query history is cleared, and dbpeek prompts for a new connection string. Your previous session's data is gone from memory at this point.

Export session log — Downloads the full in-memory query history as a JSON file to your local machine. The download is a standard browser download — the file goes wherever your browser saves downloads. This is the only time dbpeek ever writes data to disk, and it only happens if you explicitly click this button.
keywords: session report summary stats overview

title: Data diff
content:
Data diff

The data diff view compares two tables — or the results of two queries — and shows you exactly what is added, removed, or changed. Viewing a diff is read-only. Applying changes from the diff requires --write mode.

Opening the diff view

Click the Diff icon in the toolbar. A dialog prompts you to choose two sources to compare.

Comparison modes

Table vs table

Select two tables from your schema. You can compare:

- The same table in two different schemas (e.g., staging.users vs production.users)
- Any two tables that share a common join key

dbpeek runs SELECT FROM table_a and SELECT FROM table_b under the hood and computes the diff client-side.

Query vs query

Write two arbitrary SELECT statements. The diff is computed from whatever those queries return. This is useful for comparing aggregations, filtered subsets, or the output of two different joins.

Color coding

| Color | Meaning |
|-------|---------|
| Green | Row exists in the right source but not the left (added) |
| Red | Row exists in the left source but not the right (removed) |
| Amber | Row exists in both, but one or more column values differ (changed) |

For amber (changed) rows, the specific columns with differing values are highlighted within the row so you can spot the difference immediately.

Join key

Rows are matched by primary key by default. If the table has no primary key, or if you want to match on a different column, use the Join key dropdown to select any column or combination of columns.

Getting the join key right is the most important step — an incorrect join key will produce misleading results (e.g., showing all rows as added/removed when they're actually the same rows with a different ID column selected).

Practical uses

Staging vs production comparison — Verify that your staging environment has the reference data you expect before deploying.

Before / after a migration — Take a snapshot of affected rows before running a migration, then diff against the post-migration state. This works best with the query vs query mode.

Comparing two aggregation queries — Run two GROUP BY queries with different filter conditions and diff their outputs to see which groups appear in one but not the other.

Performance and row limits

The diff is computed client-side from the fetched result sets. For large tables, this can be slow and memory-intensive. If you're diffing large tables, add a LIMIT or WHERE clause to each query to keep the result sets manageable:

As a general guideline, result sets under 10,000 rows each diff instantly. Above 50,000 rows per side, you may notice a delay while the diff algorithm runs in a Web Worker.

title: CSV / JSON import
content:
CSV / JSON import

The import feature lets you load data from a local file into a database table without writing INSERT statements. All processing happens in the browser — the file never leaves your machine.

Supported formats

- CSV — any delimiter (auto-detected), with or without a header row
- JSON — an array of objects, where each object's keys map to column names

Opening the import dialog

Either:
- Click the Import button in the toolbar, or
- Drag a CSV or JSON file directly onto the results panel

Import workflow

Step 1 — Upload

Drag your file into the dialog, or click the drop zone to open a file picker. The file is read locally using the browser File API.

Step 2 — Preview

The first 10 rows of the file are shown in a preview grid. dbpeek displays the detected delimiter, row count, and column names.

Step 3 — Map columns

Each source column from the file is mapped to a destination column in the target table. dbpeek auto-maps columns by exact name match (case-insensitive). Unmapped source columns are ignored. Unmapped destination columns receive their database default value or NULL.

You can override any mapping using the dropdown for each row.

Step 4 — Choose conflict strategy

When an imported row conflicts with an existing row (e.g., duplicate primary key or unique constraint violation), dbpeek offers three strategies:

| Strategy | Behavior |
|----------|----------|
| Skip | Ignore the conflicting row and continue |
| Update (upsert) | Update the existing row with the imported values. Requires a primary key. |
| Error | Halt the entire import on the first conflict |

Step 5 — Import

Click Import to begin. All inserts run inside a single transaction. If any row fails (network error, constraint violation, type mismatch), the entire import rolls back and no rows are inserted.

A progress indicator shows the current position: "Inserting row 1,200 of 15,000..."

After completion, a success message shows the total rows inserted, or an error message identifies the failing row and the database error.

File size limits

CSV files are parsed in the browser using PapaParse. JSON files are parsed with JSON.parse(). The practical limit is approximately 50 MB in modern browsers, which covers most flat files. For files larger than this, consider splitting the file or using the database's native bulk load tool (COPY for PostgreSQL, LOAD DATA INFILE for MySQL).

Privacy

The file you import is read and parsed entirely in the browser. The raw file bytes are never sent to the Express server — only the parsed row data is sent as JSON in the POST /api/import request body, which stays on localhost.

title: Inline cell editing
content:
Inline cell editing

Inline editing lets you update a single database value without writing SQL. Double-click a cell, type the new value, confirm — done.

Editing a cell

1. Run a SELECT query that returns the table you want to edit.
2. Double-click any cell in the results grid. The cell switches to an input field with the current value pre-filled and selected.
3. Type the new value.
4. Press Enter or Tab to commit, or Escape to cancel without changes.

After you commit the new value, dbpeek generates an UPDATE statement and shows a confirmation dialog:

Click Execute to apply the change to the database, or Cancel to discard it. The change is not written until you click Execute.

Undoing a change

Press within the same session to revert the last inline edit. dbpeek generates a reverse UPDATE using the original value:

The same confirmation dialog appears. Undo is available for the current session only — there is no persistent undo history across sessions.

WHERE clause safety

The generated WHERE clause always uses the primary key of the row, never arbitrary column values. This prevents accidental mass updates. For example, if a table has a composite primary key of (orderid, lineitem_id), the WHERE clause will include both columns.

Limitations

| Limitation | Reason |
|------------|--------|
| Tables without a primary key | dbpeek cannot safely construct a single-row WHERE clause |
| Binary / BLOB columns | No sensible text representation for editing |
| Columns from JOIN results | The source table is ambiguous; dbpeek cannot determine which table to UPDATE |
| Computed columns / views | The column has no direct storage location |

If a cell is not editable due to one of these limitations, double-clicking it does nothing. Hovering shows a tooltip explaining why editing is unavailable.

Tips

- Use Tab to move between cells while staying in edit mode — this speeds up entering data across multiple columns in the same row.
- The confirmation dialog shows the exact SQL. Review it before clicking Execute, especially when editing columns that other tables reference via foreign keys.
- For bulk updates, write a SQL UPDATE statement directly in the editor — inline editing is intended for individual cell corrections.
keywords: inline edit cell edit edit row update cell

title: Data modification overview
content:
Data modification overview

All features in this section require --write or --full mode. The default read-only mode blocks all data modification. Pass the flag explicitly when starting dbpeek — for example, npx dbpeek postgres://localhost/mydb --write.

dbpeek ships with four data modification features, each gated behind an appropriate permission level.

Feature overview

Permission modes

| Mode | Flag | What it allows |
|------|------|----------------|
| Read-only | (default) | SELECT, EXPLAIN, SHOW |
| Write | --write | All of the above + INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, REPLACE, MERGE |
| Full | --full | All of the above + CREATE, DROP, ALTER, TRUNCATE, GRANT |

Safety guarantees

Every modification feature follows the same safety pattern:

1. You initiate the change through the UI
2. dbpeek generates the SQL that would be executed
3. A confirmation dialog shows the exact SQL before anything runs
4. You click Execute to apply, or Cancel to discard

All modifications are logged to query history with the same timestamp, status, and row-count information as regular queries.

Transactions

Where possible, dbpeek wraps bulk modifications in a transaction:

- CSV/JSON import — all inserts run inside a single transaction. If any row fails, the entire import rolls back.
- Table structure editor — each ALTER TABLE is executed individually (databases generally don't support transactional DDL, except PostgreSQL which does).
- Inline editing — each UPDATE is a single-statement transaction by default.

For PostgreSQL specifically, DDL inside an explicit BEGIN / COMMIT block is transactional. The table editor takes advantage of this when possible.

title: Table structure editor
content:
Table structure editor

The table structure editor lets you modify your schema without writing DDL. Changes are previewed as ALTER TABLE statements before anything executes.

Accessing the editor

The editor opens as a panel showing all current columns with their types, defaults, and constraints.

Supported operations

Add column

- Name — column name (validated against the dialect's naming rules)
- Type — select from a dialect-specific dropdown (e.g., VARCHAR, INTEGER, TIMESTAMP, JSONB)
- Default — optional default value expression
- NOT NULL — toggle the constraint on or off

Remove column

Change column type

Modify default value

Add / remove NOT NULL constraint

Toggle the NOT NULL checkbox for any column.

Preview before executing

Before any change is applied to the database, dbpeek shows the full set of generated ALTER TABLE statements:

Review the statements, then click Execute all to apply them or Cancel to discard all pending changes.

SQLite limitation

SQLite has limited ALTER TABLE support. Older SQLite versions (pre-3.35.0) do not support DROP COLUMN, and no version supports RENAME COLUMN via a simple ALTER. When you request these operations on a SQLite database, dbpeek handles them using the recommended pragma sequence: rename the original table, create the new table with the desired structure, copy data across, drop the renamed original, and update any foreign key references. This process runs inside a transaction but takes significantly longer than a simple ALTER TABLE on PostgreSQL or MySQL. Large tables may take several seconds.

Notes

- PostgreSQL DDL is transactional. If you apply multiple changes at once, they run inside a BEGIN / COMMIT block. If any step fails, all changes roll back.
- MySQL DDL is not transactional. Each ALTER TABLE statement commits immediately. If a later statement fails, earlier ones are already applied.
- MSSQL supports transactional DDL similarly to PostgreSQL.
- The table editor does not support adding or removing indexes, creating foreign keys, or modifying primary keys. For those operations, write the DDL directly in the editor with --full mode.

title: Multi-tab queries
content:
Multi-tab queries

The tab bar above the editor gives each tab its own isolated SQL workspace. Tabs are useful for keeping multiple queries in flight, comparing result sets, or working on different tables without losing your progress.

!Tab bar with three open tabs

What each tab contains

Every tab maintains its own independent state:

- SQL text — the editor content for that tab
- Query results — the last result set from running a query in that tab
- View mode — whether results are showing the grid, chart, or EXPLAIN view
- Column sort and filter state — client-side sorts and filters applied to the result grid
- Query history — the history of queries run in that tab (not shared across tabs)

Switching tabs instantly restores all of this state.

Tab management shortcuts

| Action | Mac | Windows/Linux |
|--------|-----|---------------|
| New tab | ⌘T | CtrlT |
| Close current tab | ⌘W | CtrlW |
| Switch to tab 1 | ⌘1 | Ctrl1 |
| Switch to tab 2–9 | ⌘2–9 | Ctrl2–9 |

You can also click the + button in the tab bar to open a new tab, or click the × on any tab to close it. The last remaining tab cannot be closed.

Tab names

Tabs are named automatically. The default name is derived from the first FROM clause in the current SQL:

To rename a tab, double-click the tab name. An inline input appears — type your name and press Enter.

Implementation note: single CodeMirror instance

The editor UI uses a single CodeMirror instance that hot-swaps its document state when you switch tabs. This is different from creating and destroying separate editor instances per tab.

The reason: creating a CodeMirror editor has a non-trivial startup cost — it measures fonts, computes line heights, and initializes extension state. Destroying and recreating it on every tab switch would cause a visible flash and potential font rendering artifacts.

Instead, each tab stores a CodeMirror EditorState snapshot. When you switch tabs, the editor calls view.setState(savedState) to swap in the new document, cursor position, and undo history atomically.

Tab persistence

Tab state is stored in Zustand (in-memory React state). It is not persisted to disk or localStorage.

Closing the browser tab or terminal window loses all tab content. For queries you want to keep between sessions, copy them to a .sql file in your project.

Common use cases

Comparing two queries — Run SELECT COUNT() FROM orders in tab 1 and SELECT COUNT() FROM orders WHERE status = 'completed' in tab 2. Switch between tabs to compare counts.

Background queries — Start a slow aggregation query in tab 2, then switch back to tab 1 to keep writing while it runs. Tab 2's results will be ready when you switch back.

Table exploration — Keep your main analytical query in tab 1. Use tab 2 as a scratchpad for quick SELECT * previews of tables you're looking up.

title: Parameterized queries
content:
Parameterized queries

Parameterized queries use placeholders instead of literal values. When placeholders are detected, a parameter panel appears below the editor with an input field for each one. Values are passed to the database driver separately — they are never string-concatenated into the SQL.

Placeholder styles

dbpeek supports two placeholder formats:

Positional — PostgreSQL style ($1, $2, ...)

Named — colon style (:name)

Both styles work in all four dialects. Use whichever is more readable for your query.

How to use the parameter panel

1. Write a query with placeholders in the editor.
2. The parameter panel appears automatically below the editor when a placeholder is detected.
3. Each placeholder gets a labeled input field.
4. Fill in the values and press ⌘↵ to run.

!Parameter panel with two input fields

Example workflow:

The panel shows three fields: $1, $2, $3. Fill in 2024-01-01, pro, 50 and run.

Under the hood

Parameters are passed via knex.raw(sql, params):

The database driver handles escaping. The values never touch string concatenation.

Type coercion

Parameter values are entered as text in the input fields. dbpeek infers the type before passing to the driver:

- Looks like an integer (42) → passed as Number
- Looks like a float (3.14) → passed as Number
- Looks like a boolean (true, false) → passed as Boolean
- Looks like a date (2024-01-15) → passed as Date
- Everything else → passed as String

If the automatic coercion is wrong (e.g., you want "42" as a string), quote the value in the input field: "42".

Why use parameterized queries

Prevents SQL injection — Even in --write and --full modes, injecting SQL through a parameter value is not possible because the value is never inserted into the SQL string.

Reusability — Change just the parameter values and re-run without re-editing the SQL.

Readability — The query logic is separated from the specific values being tested, making it easier to understand and share.

title: Query cancellation
content:
Query cancellation

When a query is running, the toolbar shows a red Cancel button. Click it, or press , to abort the query.

After cancellation, the results panel shows "Query cancelled" and the tab returns to its ready state. Any partial results are discarded.

How cancellation works per dialect

Cancellation mechanics differ by dialect because each database has its own concept of a "session" or "connection ID" that can be targeted externally.

Why a separate connection is needed

For PostgreSQL, MySQL, and MSSQL: the primary database connection is blocked waiting for the query to complete. A second, independent connection is used to issue the cancel command. Both connections must reference the same backend session ID (PID, connection ID, or SPID) that was recorded when the query started.

SQLite cancellation

SQLite runs the query synchronously inside the Node.js event loop. There is no separate connection or OS-level process to target. Instead, db.interrupt() (a better-sqlite3 method) sets an internal flag in the SQLite library. SQLite checks this flag at regular intervals during execution (between VM instructions in the bytecode engine) and throws an SQLITE_INTERRUPT error when it sees it.

Because JavaScript is single-threaded, the cancel request reaches the server only after the current synchronous call yields — which SQLite does during long table scans. For very short queries, cancellation may arrive after the query completes naturally.

After cancellation

- The results panel displays: Query cancelled by user
- The tab returns to the ready state (no spinner, Run button re-enabled)
- The database connection is left open and ready for the next query (except MSSQL, where a new connection is established)
- Query history records the cancelled query with a "cancelled" status

title: Installation
content:
Installation

dbpeek requires no installation. Run it directly with your package manager's execute command.

System requirements

- Node.js 18 or later — check with node --version
- Any modern browser — Chrome, Firefox, Safari, Edge (all current versions)
- Network access to your database — dbpeek connects from your machine, not from a server

If you're on Node 16 or older, upgrade Node first. The fetch API used by the server-side schema loader requires Node 18+.

Running dbpeek

npx (comes with npm)

pnpm

bunx

yarn

All four commands do the same thing: download the package if not cached, then run it. There's no global install step.

What happens when you run it

1. Download — npx fetches dbpeek from the npm registry (one-time per version; cached for subsequent runs).
2. Server start — An Express server starts on a random port between 3000 and 3999.
3. Browser open — Your default browser opens automatically at localhost:{port}/app.
4. Schema load — The server queries your database's information schema in the background. This takes 0.1–2 seconds depending on how many tables exist.

Troubleshooting first run

"Cannot find module 'better-sqlite3'"

This happens with SQLite connections. better-sqlite3 is a native Node add-on that needs to be compiled for your platform. Fix:

Port conflicts

dbpeek scans ports 3000–3999 in order and uses the first available one. If all are taken (unlikely), it exits with an error listing the range. Free up a port or wait for a process to finish.

Browser doesn't open

Some environments (SSH sessions, WSL without a display) can't open a browser automatically. Copy the URL printed in the terminal and open it manually:

Slow first run

The initial npx invocation downloads ~5 MB. Subsequent runs use the npm cache and start in under a second.

title: Permission modes
content:
Permission modes

dbpeek enforces a permission mode for every session. The mode is set at startup via a CLI flag and cannot be changed from the browser.

Overview

| Mode | Flag | Allowed operations |
|------|------|--------------------|
| Read-only | (default) | SELECT, EXPLAIN, SHOW, DESCRIBE, PRAGMA, WITH (CTE), VALUES |
| Write | --write | Read-only + INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, REPLACE, MERGE, UPSERT |
| Full | --full | Write + CREATE, DROP, ALTER, TRUNCATE, GRANT, REVOKE, EXEC, CALL, EXECUTE |

Read-only mode (default)

No flag required. This is the default when you run npx dbpeek .

Allowed: SELECT, WITH (CTEs), SHOW, DESCRIBE, EXPLAIN, EXPLAIN ANALYZE, PRAGMA, VALUES

Blocked: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, DROP, CREATE, ALTER, TRUNCATE, GRANT, REVOKE, EXEC, CALL, and all other write operations.

Use read-only mode when:
- Inspecting a production database
- Sharing a dbpeek session with a teammate who should not modify data
- Auditing a schema without risk of accidental changes

Write mode

Allowed: Everything in read-only mode, plus: INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, REPLACE, MERGE, UPSERT

Blocked: CREATE, DROP, ALTER, TRUNCATE, GRANT, REVOKE, EXEC, CALL

Use write mode when:
- Importing data into an existing table
- Fixing individual records directly
- Running cleanup DELETE queries

Full mode

Allowed: Everything in write mode, plus: CREATE, DROP, ALTER, TRUNCATE, GRANT, REVOKE, EXEC, CALL, EXECUTE

Use full mode when:
- Running migrations manually
- Making schema changes (adding columns, creating indexes)
- Executing stored procedures

Full mode allows destructive DDL statements like DROP TABLE and TRUNCATE. Use it only when you need to make schema changes, and prefer a database user with limited privileges even in full mode.

How the permission check works

The check happens in src/server/permissions.ts before any query reaches the database driver. The flow is:

1. The browser sends a query to POST /api/query
2. The server parses the SQL into a statement list
3. Each statement is classified by its leading keyword
4. If any statement is not permitted by the current mode, the entire batch is rejected with a 403 response and an error message identifying the blocked statement
5. Only if all statements pass does the server forward the query to the database driver

The mode value is captured as a closure variable when the Express server initializes. There is no HTTP endpoint that can change it — a browser cannot escalate its own permissions.

Multi-statement batches

If you run multiple statements separated by semicolons, all of them must be permitted:

The entire batch is blocked, even though the SELECT would be permitted on its own.

Database-level isolation

Permission modes are enforced at the application layer, not at the database layer. A determined user with access to the process could bypass them. For stronger isolation — especially in production — use a read-only database user.

This gives you database-enforced read-only access regardless of which mode dbpeek is started with.

CLI flags

title: FAQ
content:
FAQ

Is dbpeek free?

Yes. dbpeek is MIT licensed. Free forever. There is no "pro" tier, no feature gating behind a paywall, and no sign-up required. Run it with npx and you're done.

What operating systems does dbpeek support?

macOS, Linux, and Windows (including WSL2). Anywhere Node.js 18 or later runs.

Can I use dbpeek with a Docker database?

Yes. Connect to any host reachable from your machine. If the Docker container has a published port, use the forwarded port:

If the container isn't port-forwarded, use the container's internal IP (find it with docker inspect ).

Where are my credentials stored?

Nowhere. The connection string is passed as a CLI argument, parsed into a ConnectionConfig object in Node.js process memory, and cleared when the process exits. dbpeek writes no files during normal operation. There is no ~/.dbpeek/ directory, no SQLite session cache, no Keychain entry, and no environment variable written to disk. See the Privacy model page for a detailed explanation and verification steps.

How is dbpeek different from psql?

psql is a terminal client: text-only output, PostgreSQL-only, requires learning backslash commands. dbpeek gives you a visual schema tree, EXPLAIN visualizations, a multi-tab editor with syntax highlighting, one-click CSV/JSON export, chart visualization, and the same UI across all four supported SQL dialects.

That said, psql has scripting superpowers dbpeek will never match — variable interpolation, \copy, conditional execution with \if, and the ability to pipe SQL scripts from the shell. They complement each other rather than replace each other.

Can a non-developer use dbpeek?

If they can open a terminal and paste a command, yes. The UI after launch is entirely visual and doesn't require knowledge of SQL syntax to browse tables, view data, or export results.

Will you add MongoDB / Redis / Cassandra support?

No. dbpeek is explicitly SQL-only by design. Supporting NoSQL databases would require a fundamentally different query model, schema representation, and permission system — it would become a different product. See Supported databases for the full rationale.

Will you add AI / natural language to SQL?

No. Any NL-to-SQL feature would need to send your query text — and likely your schema — to a third-party API. This breaks dbpeek's core design principle: no data leaves localhost. The privacy model is not negotiable.

Can I run dbpeek as a persistent server for my team?

dbpeek is designed as a single-user CLI tool, not a persistent shared server. For a shared team SQL client, consider TablePlus (server mode), Metabase, or Redash. For a self-hosted option with user management, Metabase Community Edition is free.

How does dbpeek handle large result sets?

Results are paginated in the UI. By default, dbpeek fetches up to 1,000 rows and displays them in the grid with virtual scrolling. To get more rows, add a LIMIT clause or use the export feature (which streams all rows to a file without loading them all into the browser at once).

How do I report a bug or request a feature?

Open an issue at github.com/alvinwquach/dbpeek/issues. Include:

- The error message or unexpected behavior
- Your Node.js version (node --version)
- Your operating system and version
- The dbpeek version (npx dbpeek --version)
- The database dialect you were connecting to (no credentials needed)

title: Supported databases
content:
Supported databases

dbpeek supports four SQL dialects. Each dialect uses a battle-tested Node.js driver under the hood; dbpeek does not implement its own wire protocol.

Supported dialects

| Dialect | Min Version | Driver | Default Port | Notes |
|---------|-------------|--------|--------------|-------|
| PostgreSQL | 12+ | pg (node-postgres) | 5432 | pgvector extension supported |
| MySQL | 5.7+ | mysql2 | 3306 | MariaDB 10.3+ compatible |
| SQLite | 3.x | better-sqlite3 | (file path) | :memory: databases supported |
| MSSQL | SQL Server 2017+ | tedious | 1433 | Azure SQL Database supported |

PostgreSQL notes

- PostgreSQL 12 is the minimum because EXPLAIN format improvements in 12 are required for the plan visualizer.
- pgvector columns (vector type) display as arrays in the results grid.
- LISTEN / NOTIFY is not supported — dbpeek uses HTTP polling, not persistent connections.

MySQL notes

- MySQL 5.7 is supported for basic usage. EXPLAIN ANALYZE (visual plans) requires MySQL 8.0.18+.
- MariaDB 10.3+ is compatible for most features. Some EXPLAIN output differences may affect the plan visualizer.
- PlanetScale is compatible via its MySQL-compatible API (see hosted platforms below).

SQLite notes

- Connects to a file path: sqlite:///absolute/path/to/file.db
- In-memory databases (sqlite://:memory:) are supported and useful for testing.
- The native better-sqlite3 addon requires a C++ build toolchain. See Troubleshooting if you get a build error.

MSSQL notes

- SQL Server 2017+ is required. Azure SQL Database is fully supported.
- Windows Authentication (Kerberos/SSPI) is not currently supported — use SQL Server authentication.
- The connection string uses the mssql:// scheme regardless of whether the server is on-premises or Azure.

Tested hosting platforms

| Platform | Dialect | Notes |
|----------|---------|-------|
| Supabase | PostgreSQL | Add ?sslmode=require to the connection string |
| Neon | PostgreSQL | Add ?sslmode=require; serverless cold starts may add ~500ms |
| PlanetScale | MySQL | MySQL-compatible API; use standard MySQL connection string |
| Railway | PostgreSQL / MySQL | Copy the connection string from the Railway dashboard |
| AWS RDS | PostgreSQL / MySQL / MSSQL | Standard connection strings; ensure security group allows your IP |
| Azure SQL | MSSQL | Standard MSSQL connection string; use SQL auth |
| Fly.io | PostgreSQL | Works with Fly Postgres or an attached Supabase instance |
| Render | PostgreSQL / MySQL | Standard connection strings from the Render dashboard |

Not supported

dbpeek is explicitly SQL-only. The following databases are not supported and are not planned:

- MongoDB — document model, no SQL
- Redis — key-value store, no SQL
- Cassandra — CQL is SQL-like but not compatible with the SQL permission model dbpeek enforces
- DynamoDB — proprietary API, no SQL

See the FAQ for more context on this decision.

title: Troubleshooting
content:
Troubleshooting

Cannot find module 'better-sqlite3'

SQLite requires a native C++ addon that must be compiled for your specific platform and Node.js version. You'll see this error if the prebuilt binary for your platform isn't available.

Solution:

1. Install the build toolchain:
 - macOS: xcode-select --install
 - Windows: Install "Build Tools for Visual Studio" from the Visual Studio downloads page
 - Linux: sudo apt-get install build-essential python3 (Debian/Ubuntu) or equivalent
2. Install node-gyp globally: npm install -g node-gyp
3. Retry: npx dbpeek sqlite:///path/to/file.db

If you're on an Apple Silicon Mac and the error persists, ensure you're running the arm64 build of Node.js (not Rosetta x64): node -p process.arch should print arm64.

EADDRINUSE: address already in use :::3000

Port 3000 is occupied by another process. dbpeek normally tries ports 3000–3999 automatically and picks the first available one. If all ports in the range are occupied, or if you requested a specific port with --port, you'll see this error.

Solutions:

Connection refused (localhost PostgreSQL)

Symptom: connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:5432

Fix 1: Use 127.0.0.1 instead of localhost in the connection string:

On some systems, localhost resolves to IPv6 ::1, but PostgreSQL listens only on IPv4 127.0.0.1. Using the literal IP address bypasses DNS resolution.

Fix 2: Verify PostgreSQL is running:

If PostgreSQL isn't running, start it with your system's service manager (brew services start postgresql, systemctl start postgresql, etc.).

SSL errors with hosted PostgreSQL

Symptom: SSL SYSCALL error: EOF detected or SELFSIGNEDCERTINCHAIN

Most hosted PostgreSQL providers require SSL. Add ?sslmode=require to your connection string:

To disable SSL certificate verification (for self-signed certs in development — not recommended for production):

Browser doesn't open automatically

dbpeek always prints the URL to stdout. If your browser doesn't open, copy the URL and open it manually. It is typically:

To always suppress the auto-open behavior: npx dbpeek ... --no-open

Autocomplete not showing

Schema introspection runs in the background after the connection is established. Wait 1–2 seconds for it to complete, then try again. If autocomplete never appears:

1. Check the terminal for schema fetch errors — they appear as [schema] error: ... log lines.
2. Verify your database user has SELECT permission on information_schema (or the dialect equivalent).

Query times out

The connection pool uses a default statement timeout of 30 seconds. For long-running queries:

1. Open the EXPLAIN plan first () to understand the query plan and identify bottlenecks.
2. Press to cancel a running query.
3. For legitimate long queries (migrations, large exports), consider running them directly in psql or the equivalent CLI tool where you can set a custom statement timeout.

"EPERM: operation not permitted" on SQLite

The SQLite file is read-only or owned by another user. Check the file permissions:

If the file is on a network volume, copy it locally before connecting — some network filesystems don't support the file locking that SQLite requires.

title: Chart visualization
content:
Chart visualization

Click the Chart icon in the results view toggle (next to the grid icon) to switch from the data grid to a chart view of the same result set. No additional query is run — the chart uses the data already fetched.

!Bar chart showing order counts by status

Auto-detection logic

dbpeek inspects the column types in your result set and picks a chart type automatically:

| Column pattern | Chart type |
|----------------|------------|
| 1 text/category column + 1 numeric column | Bar chart — text on X axis, number on Y |
| 1 date/timestamp column + 1+ numeric columns | Line chart — time series, one line per numeric column |
| 2 numeric columns | Scatter plot — first column on X, second on Y |
| Any other combination | Bar chart — first column on X, second column on Y |

Example queries and their chart types

Manual axis override

If the auto-detection picks the wrong chart, use the X-axis and Y-axis pickers in the chart toolbar to choose any columns from the result set. The chart re-renders immediately.

For line charts with multiple numeric columns (multiple series), use the Series picker to add or remove series.

Chart library

Charts are built with Recharts, a React-native charting library. Features:

- Hover tooltips — hover over any data point to see the exact X and Y values
- Legend — shown when there are multiple series (multiple lines on a line chart)
- Responsive sizing — the chart fills its container and redraws on window resize
- Animated entry — bars and lines animate in on first render (can be disabled in settings)

Limitations

Maximum 10,000 data points — If the result set has more than 10,000 rows, the chart renders a downsampled version using reservoir sampling. A warning is shown: Showing 10,000 of 48,203 rows. The full data is still available in the grid view.

No server-side aggregation — Charts use the result set as-is. For large time-series datasets, pre-aggregate in SQL for best results:

This fetches 90 rows instead of potentially millions, and the chart renders instantly.

No chart configuration persistence — Chart type and axis selections reset when you run a new query or switch tabs.

title: Copy cell / copy row
content:
Copy cell / copy row

Right-clicking any cell in the results grid opens a context menu with copy options at multiple granularities.

Context menu options

Copy cell value — copies the raw value of the clicked cell as plain text.

Copy row as JSON — copies the entire row as a JSON object:

Keys are the column names. Values use their JavaScript types (numbers stay numbers, booleans stay booleans).

Copy row as CSV — copies the row as comma-separated values with a header line:

Copy column as CSV — copies all values in the clicked column (with header) as newline-separated values:

Select row — selects the row for keyboard navigation without triggering a copy.

Keyboard shortcuts

| Action | Mac | Windows/Linux |
|--------|-----|---------------|
| Copy selected cell | ⌘C | CtrlC |
| Navigate between cells | ←→↑↓ | ←→↑↓ |

Arrow key navigation moves the selection between cells in the results grid. ⌘C copies the currently selected cell's value.

NULL value handling

| Format | NULL representation |
|--------|---------------------|
| Cell value | empty string |
| Row as JSON | null (JSON null) |
| Row as CSV | empty field (two consecutive commas, or trailing comma) |
| Column as CSV | empty line for that row |

Clipboard API

All copy operations use navigator.clipboard.writeText(). This API requires either:

- A secure context (HTTPS), or
- localhost (which is considered secure)

Since dbpeek always runs on localhost, clipboard access works without any additional permissions. If you're accessing dbpeek through a proxy or tunnel that changes the origin, clipboard operations may fail silently — in that case, use the value viewer's Copy button instead.

Copying multiple rows

To copy multiple rows at once, select them first using click + Shift+click (range selection), then right-click and choose Copy selected rows as JSON or Copy selected rows as CSV. The output includes one JSON object or CSV line per selected row.

title: Export (CSV / JSON / Excel)
content:
Export (CSV / JSON / Excel)

Click the download icon in the results toolbar to open the export menu. Choose a format and the file downloads immediately to your browser's default download location.

Formats

CSV

- Encoding: UTF-8 with BOM (for compatibility with Excel on Windows)
- Standard: RFC 4180 compliant
- Fields containing commas, quotes, or newlines are wrapped in double quotes
- Embedded double quotes are escaped as ""
- NULL values become empty strings (no representation in CSV for null)
- First row is the header row (column names)
- Filename: query-2024-01-15-14-30.csv

Example:

JSON

- Format: array of objects
- Types are preserved: numbers stay numbers, booleans stay booleans, NULL becomes null
- Date/timestamp columns become ISO 8601 strings: "2024-01-15T14:30:00.000Z"
- Filename: query-2024-01-15-14-30.json

Example:

Excel (.xlsx)

Built with the xlsx library (SheetJS):

- Numbers stay as numeric cells (not text-formatted numbers)
- Booleans become Excel TRUE/FALSE
- Dates become Excel date values (displayed according to the cell format, not as ISO strings)
- NULL becomes an empty cell
- Column headers in row 1 with bold formatting
- Filename: query-2024-01-15-14-30.xlsx

What gets exported

The export contains the currently visible rows — after any active client-side sorts and filters. If you have filtered the results to 23 of 1,204 rows, the export contains 23 rows in the current sort order.

To export all rows regardless of filters, click Clear all filters in the results toolbar before exporting.

File naming

Export filenames use the format: query-YYYY-MM-DD-HH-mm.{ext} — the timestamp is the local time when you clicked export.

Large exports

All three formats are generated in the browser from the in-memory result set. Performance characteristics:

| Format | 10K rows | 100K rows | 1M rows |
|--------|----------|-----------|---------|
| CSV | 
Exporting very large result sets (500K+ rows) may cause the browser tab to become unresponsive for several seconds while the file is being generated. For data exports of that scale, consider using your database's native export tools (pg_dump, mysqldump, etc.) instead.

Exports are generated entirely in the browser. The file never passes through any server or third-party service — it goes directly from browser memory to your local filesystem.

title: Results grid
content:
Results grid

Query results are rendered in a TanStack Table (v8) grid with full row virtualization via @tanstack/react-virtual. Only rows in the current viewport are in the DOM — scrolling a million-row result set at 60fps is normal.

!Results grid showing a multi-column query result

Performance

The virtual scroller renders approximately 30 rows at a time (enough to fill the viewport plus a small buffer above and below). As you scroll, rows are mounted and unmounted dynamically. Row height is fixed at 32px for consistent scroll behavior.

For most queries (⌘A — selects all rows
- Click another row — moves selection; does not multi-select (Shift+click for range selection)

Selected rows are used by the copy row commands in the right-click context menu.

Fixed header and scrolling

The header row is sticky and does not scroll with the data. Horizontal scrolling (for wide result sets) scrolls both the header row and data rows together, keeping columns aligned.

Row count

The total row count is always shown below the results grid. When client-side filters are active, it shows: 23 of 1,204 rows.

title: Sorting & filtering
content:
Sorting & filtering

Sorting and filtering in the results grid are client-side operations on the data already loaded into the browser. They do not issue new queries to the database.

Sorting

Click any column header to sort the results by that column. Each click cycles through three states:

1. Ascending (↑ arrow) — lowest to highest, A to Z, oldest to newest
2. Descending (↓ arrow) — highest to lowest, Z to A, newest to oldest
3. Unsorted (no arrow) — original query order

Only one column can be the active sort column at a time. Clicking a different column header replaces the previous sort.

Sort order is type-aware:
- Numeric columns — sorted numerically (so 10 comes after 9, not after 1)
- Date/timestamp columns — sorted chronologically
- Text columns — sorted lexicographically (case-insensitive)
- NULL values — sorted to the bottom in both ascending and descending order

Column filtering

Click the filter icon (funnel icon) next to any column header to reveal a text input for that column.

- Type to filter rows: only rows where the column value contains the typed text are shown
- Matching is case-insensitive and substring-based (ord matches orders, reordered, etc.)
- Multiple column filters are ANDed: a row must pass all active filters to be shown

The filtered row count updates as you type:

Clearing filters

- Click the × in any filter input to clear that one filter
- Click the Clear all filters button (appears in the results toolbar when any filter is active) to remove all filters at once

Interaction between sort and filter

Sorting applies to the filtered subset. If you filter to 23 rows and then sort by a column, only those 23 rows are reordered.

Client-side vs server-side

Sorting and filtering are intentionally client-side. This keeps the interaction instantaneous (no network wait) for result sets that fit in browser memory.

For result sets too large to load in full, use SQL to do the filtering and ordering before fetching:

This avoids loading rows you don't need and gives you the database's index-optimized sorting.

Export with active filters

When you export results (CSV, JSON, or Excel), the export contains only the currently visible rows — after all active sorts and filters. If you have filtered to 23 rows, the export contains 23 rows. See Export → for details.

title: Value viewer
content:
Value viewer

The results grid truncates long cell values for performance. Click any cell to open the value viewer panel, which shows the complete value formatted for its content type.

!Value viewer panel showing a formatted JSON value

Auto-detected content types

The value viewer inspects the cell content and renders it accordingly:

JSON

If the value parses as valid JSON, it is displayed as a collapsible tree:

- Objects and arrays are collapsed by default
- Click the expand arrow to open a node
- Keys are colored differently from values
- Primitive values (strings, numbers, booleans, null) are shown with type-appropriate colors

Binary / bytea

Binary columns (PostgreSQL bytea, MySQL BLOB, etc.) are shown as a hex dump:

The offset column helps locate specific byte positions in large binary values.

Long text

Text values longer than 256 characters are shown with:

- Line numbers in the gutter
- Word wrap enabled
- Monospace font for readability

URLs

If the value starts with http:// or https://, it is rendered as a clickable link that opens in a new tab.

Dates and timestamps

Shown as two lines:
1. Formatted date: January 15, 2024 at 2:30:45 PM UTC
2. Raw value: 2024-01-15T14:30:45.000Z

Regular values

All other values are shown as plain text in a monospace font with a copy button.

Keyboard shortcuts

| Action | Shortcut |
|--------|----------|
| Close the value viewer | Esc |
| Copy the raw value | ⌘C |

Copy button

The Copy button in the value viewer header copies the complete raw value — not the formatted display. For a JSON value, this means the raw JSON string (not the tree rendering). For a timestamp, this means the raw database value.

Why the value viewer exists

The grid truncates values for two reasons:

1. Performance — rendering thousands of long strings in the DOM is slow
2. Layout — very long values would make rows unreadably tall or overflow columns

The value viewer solves both: cells stay compact in the grid, and full values are one click away. No additional database query is made — the viewer reads the value already in memory from the query result.

title: Column statistics
content:
Column statistics

Click any column name in the schema explorer tree to open the column statistics panel. The panel shows aggregated statistics for that column, computed by running a single query against the live table.

!Column statistics panel for a text column

Statistics by column type

All columns

| Stat | Description |
|------|-------------|
| Distinct count | COUNT(DISTINCT col) — exact count of unique non-null values |
| Null % | Percentage of rows where the column is NULL |
| Total rows | COUNT(*) for the table (used to compute null %) |

Numeric columns

Additional stats for INTEGER, BIGINT, NUMERIC, FLOAT, DECIMAL, and similar types:

| Stat | Description |
|------|-------------|
| Min | MIN(col) |
| Max | MAX(col) |
| Avg | AVG(col) rounded to 4 decimal places |
| Stddev | STDDEV(col) (or STDEV for MSSQL) |

Text columns

For VARCHAR, TEXT, CHAR, and similar types, the top 10 most frequent values are shown with their counts:

Date and timestamp columns

| Stat | Description |
|------|-------------|
| Min date | Earliest value in the column |
| Max date | Most recent value in the column |
| Range | Human-readable span: "3 years, 4 months" |

How the query works

dbpeek runs a single aggregation query per column. For a text column, it looks like:

The top-values query is a separate GROUP BY:

Both queries are run in sequence on demand. They are not pre-computed at schema load time.

Caching

Results are cached per column for the duration of the session. Re-clicking the same column returns the cached result instantly. To refresh (e.g., after inserting new rows), hold ⌥ and click the column name — this bypasses the cache and re-runs the queries.

Practical uses

- Before writing a GROUP BY — check distinct count to decide if the column is a good grouping key
- Before adding an index — check null % and distinct count to evaluate index selectivity
- Data quality checks — find unexpected nulls or an unexpectedly small distinct count on a column that should be unique
- Date range awareness — see the span of data before writing date-range filters

title: DDL viewer
content:
DDL viewer

The DDL viewer shows the CREATE TABLE statement for any table in your schema. Open it by right-clicking a table in the schema explorer and choosing Show DDL.

The statement opens in a read-only modal with SQL syntax highlighting and a Copy button.

!DDL viewer modal showing a CREATE TABLE statement

What's included

The DDL includes:

- Column definitions: name, data type, length/precision, NOT NULL, DEFAULT values
- Primary key constraint
- Unique constraints
- Check constraints
- Foreign key references
- Index definitions (as separate CREATE INDEX statements below the table)

How DDL is retrieved per dialect

Syntax highlighting

The DDL is rendered using the same CodeMirror SQL highlighter as the editor. Keywords like CREATE, TABLE, PRIMARY KEY, and REFERENCES are highlighted in the same color scheme.

Copying the DDL

Click the Copy button in the modal header to copy the full DDL statement to your clipboard. The copied text is the raw SQL — not the highlighted HTML.

Common uses

- Understanding a table you didn't create — see exactly what constraints and defaults were set without writing any queries
- Migrating a table to another database — copy the DDL and adapt it to the target dialect
- Documentation — paste the DDL into a schema reference document
- Debugging foreign key issues — see all REFERENCES clauses at once to trace the relationship graph
keywords: ddl create table definition schema sql

title: ERD diagrams
content:
ERD diagrams

The ERD (entity relationship diagram) view renders your database schema as an interactive node graph. Tables are nodes; foreign key relationships are directed edges.

Click the ERD icon in the top toolbar to open the ERD canvas.

!ERD canvas showing tables connected by foreign key edges

What's shown

Nodes — one per table:
- Table name in the node header
- All columns listed below the header with their data types
- Primary key columns are highlighted

Edges — one per foreign key:
- Directed from the child table (the one with the FK column) to the parent table
- Labeled with the column name(s) involved in the relationship
- Arrow points toward the referenced (parent) table

How foreign keys are detected

Layout

Nodes are positioned automatically using the Dagre directed graph layout algorithm. Dagre arranges nodes to minimize edge crossings and produces a top-down hierarchy where parent tables appear above child tables.

Interacting with the diagram

| Interaction | Result |
|-------------|--------|
| Drag a node | Reposition it; other nodes stay in place |
| Scroll / pinch | Zoom in and out |
| Click a node | Highlight it and its direct neighbors; all other nodes dim |
| Double-click a node | Load that table's first 100 rows in the results panel |
| Click canvas background | Deselect; all nodes return to full opacity |

Use the zoom controls in the bottom-left corner of the canvas to fit all nodes to the viewport, or zoom to a specific level.

Large schemas

For databases with many tables, the ERD can become dense. Use the search input above the canvas to filter nodes by table name — matching tables stay visible; others are hidden (edges to hidden tables are also hidden).

Alternatively, pin the tables you care about in the schema explorer first, then use the Show pinned only toggle in the ERD toolbar to render only pinned tables and the relationships between them.
keywords: erd entity relationship diagram foreign keys relations

title: Schema explorer
content:
Schema explorer

The left sidebar is the schema explorer. It shows every table in the connected database in a collapsible tree. Schema data is fetched once at connect time from information_schema (or the dialect equivalent) and cached for the session.

!Schema explorer sidebar showing table list with expanded columns

Column badges

When you expand a table, each column shows its name, data type, and up to three constraint badges:

- PK — primary key (blue pill)
- FK — foreign key (amber pill)
- IX — indexed column (muted gray pill)

A column can show multiple badges (e.g., a foreign key that is also indexed shows both FK and IX).

Row count estimates

Each table name is followed by a row count estimate. These are fetched from database catalog tables for speed — not from a full COUNT(*):

| Dialect | Source |
|---------|--------|
| PostgreSQL | pg_class.reltuples — updated by ANALYZE, fast but approximate |
| MySQL | informationschema.tables.TABLEROWS — approximate for InnoDB |
| SQLite | SELECT COUNT(*) FROM {table} — exact, run on schema load |
| MSSQL | sys.dmdbpartitionstats.rowcount — approximate |

For SQLite, counts are exact but may add to schema load time on large databases. For other dialects, estimates can be slightly stale if the table was recently modified without running ANALYZE.

Search

The search input at the top of the sidebar filters the table list in real time. It matches against:

- Table names — ord matches orders, order_items, backorders
- Column names — created matches any table that has a column containing "created"

Matching is case-insensitive. The filtered view still shows all columns when you expand a matched table.

One-click table preview

Click any table name to load its first 100 rows into the results panel. This is equivalent to:

The query is run immediately — no need to switch to the editor first. This is the fastest way to inspect a table's contents.

Right-click context menu

Right-clicking a table in the sidebar opens a context menu with:

- Preview table — same as clicking the table name
- Pin to top — moves this table to the Pinned section at the top of the sidebar (see Pin tables →)
- Show DDL — opens the DDL viewer modal (see DDL viewer →)
- Copy table name — copies the table identifier to the clipboard

Refreshing the schema

The schema is cached when dbpeek connects. If you add or drop tables during the session (in --full mode), click the Refresh icon (circular arrow) at the top of the sidebar. This re-queries information_schema and rebuilds the tree and autocomplete source without restarting.
keywords: schema tables browse tree database objects

title: Pin tables
content:
Pin tables

In databases with many tables, scrolling through the full list to find the five you care about is slow. Pinning moves your most-used tables to a dedicated Pinned section at the very top of the schema explorer, above all other tables.

How to pin a table

Right-click any table in the schema explorer → Pin to top.

The table immediately appears in the Pinned section at the top of the sidebar. It also stays in its original position in the All tables section below.

!Schema sidebar with a Pinned section showing two tables

How to unpin a table

Right-click the table (in either the Pinned section or All tables) → Unpin.

The Pinned section disappears from the sidebar when there are no pinned tables.

Pinned section behavior

The pinned section works identically to the main table list:

- Click a table name to preview its first 100 rows
- Expand the table to see columns with type and constraint badges
- Right-click to access the full context menu (Show DDL, Copy table name, etc.)
- The same row count estimate is shown

Pinning multiple tables

There is no limit on the number of pinned tables. Pin as many as needed. The pinned section scrolls independently if the list is long.

Session scope

Pins are stored in Zustand (in-memory state). They are not persisted to disk, localStorage, or any config file.

Closing the terminal or browser window clears all pins. The next session starts with an empty pinned section.

No information about which tables you pinned is written to disk or sent anywhere. Like all dbpeek state, pins exist only in the browser's JavaScript memory for the current session.

Use case: large multi-tenant schema

In a database with 200+ tables across multiple services, pinning the 4–5 tables relevant to your current task keeps them instantly accessible without scrolling or searching. Combined with the sidebar search, you can find any table quickly even in very large schemas.
keywords: pin bookmark favorite quick access
